source_note: Compiled from publicly-reported PWC Planning Commission and Board of County Supervisors votes on data-center rezonings and special use permits between Dec 2023 and May 2026. Source articles: insidenova.com, princewilliamtimes.com, potomaclocal.com, datacenterdynamics.com, wtop.com, datacenterfrontier.com, wusa9.com, dcist.com, washingtonpost.com, valawyersweekly.com.

pages.text: PW DIGITAL GATEWAY (Pageland Lane / western PWC near Gainesville) — REZONING APPROVED DECEMBER 13 2023. The Prince William Board of County Supervisors voted 4-3 in favor of the PW Digital Gateway rezoning after a 27-hour public hearing, approving roughly 23 million square feet of data centers on approximately 2,100 acres along Pageland Lane in the western part of the county near Gainesville. Democratic Supervisor Kenny Boddye of the Occoquan District abstained. All three Republican supervisors dissented; the Democratic majority carried the vote. The corridor is intended to be built out over the next two decades and is described as expected to become the largest data-center corridor in the world. Developers: Compass Data Centers and QTS. LEGAL HISTORY: In August 2025, a state judge ruled the rezoning void ab initio on the basis that the county failed to follow its own public-notification ordinances for the December 2023 hearing. In October 2025, the Virginia Court of Appeals stayed that ruling and reinstated the rezonings while the county's appeal played out, allowing Compass and QTS to resume pre-construction work. On April 14 2026 the BOCS voted unanimously NOT to file a petition for a writ of appeal to the Supreme Court of Virginia on the Court of Appeals' decision. The board has also approved additional $400,000 in litigation funding for the related court cases.

HORNBAKER ROAD DATA CENTER (Brentsville District, ±40 acres near Innovation Town Center) — SUP2025-00016 AND REZONING APPROVED. The Board of County Supervisors voted 4-3 in favor on the Hornbaker Road data center after Planning Commission denial. Voting AGAINST at BOCS: Chair Deshundra Jefferson, Coles District Supervisor Yesli Vega, Gainesville Supervisor George Stewart. Voting FOR: the other four supervisors. Applicants: 'MJV Parcel A, LLC' and 'PWC – Parcel B, LLC'. The action rezoned approximately 40 acres from A-1 (agricultural) and PBD (planned business district) to M-2 (light industrial). Nearby townhouses sit approximately 400-450 feet away. Expected employment: 250-300 positions associated with chip manufacturer MobileSentrix. A last-minute proffer addition addressed the nearby Pegasus substation, mandating that no new transmission line infrastructure would be required for the project. Supervisor Stewart characterized the project as 'putting lipstick on a pig.' Chair Jefferson stated the board 'lacked the political will' to reject it. PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (November 5 2025): Planning Commission voted 4-3 to DENY. Voting to deny: Christopher Carroll (Brentsville), Mark Scheufler, Karla Justice, Blake Ross. Voting to approve: Juan McPhail (Chair), Qwendolyn Brown (Vice Chair), Cynthia Moses-Nedd. Commissioner Sheikh absent. Commissioners cited that the parcel had been intentionally removed from the Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District in 2019 and wanted to preserve the area for the county's original Innovation Park / Innovation District vision (non-data buildings). Represented at PC by land-use attorney Lee Gleason. CONTEXT: this parcel sits across Prince William Parkway from Innovation Town Center in the Brentsville District.

MID-COUNTY INDUSTRIAL PARK DATA CENTERS (intersection of VA-234 and Minnieville Road) — REZONING APPROVED 5-3. The Board of County Supervisors approved a rezoning that would allow three data centers up to 95 feet tall on approximately 64 acres just north of the VA-234 / Minnieville Road intersection. Vote was 5-3 in favor. This was described as the second mid-county data-center project approved by the board. GEORGE MASON UNIVERSITY EDGE (REZ2023-00001) — PLANNING COMMISSION 4-3 FAVORABLE RECOMMENDATION (July 2025). Applicant: JK Holdings. Proposed: a 577,000 square foot data center up to 80 feet tall at the corner of Prince William Parkway and University Boulevard, directly across from planned George Mason University student housing and commercial development in the Innovation District. The Planning Commission voted 4-3 to recommend BOCS approval. Opposition raised concerns about cumulative impacts from data-center proliferation, diesel-generator reliance during peak demand periods (air quality and noise), grid capacity challenges requiring new substations and transmission lines, and the location's misalignment with the county's stated vision for the Innovation District. One resident: 'Everybody will be impacted by this kind of unprecedented growth that seems to have no guard rails.' Coverage noted over 88 million square feet of data-center development envisioned for Prince William County in the pipeline. PC Supervisor Victor Angry received a $20,000 donation from an individual connected to JK Holdings for a Juneteenth celebration event.

ASHTON DATA CENTER (REZ2022-00031) — STAFF RECOMMENDED DENIAL. The Ashton Data Center rezoning request covers approximately 51.85 acres being rezoned from A-1 (Agricultural) and R-6 (Residential) to M/T (Industrial/Transportation) with an associated 110-foot height modification. Staff recommendation was for DENIAL dated 06/26/2024. Per the county DAPS schedule, the case had not been heard by Planning Commission or BOCS as of 01/21/2025. DEVLIN ROAD / DUMFRIES (PRINCE WILLIAM FOREST PARK EDGE) — 4 DATA CENTERS PROPOSED. Developers proposed four data centers at the edge of Prince William Forest Park, near Dumfries. The Dumfries data-center developer subsequently filed a lawsuit against PWC Chair Deshundra Jefferson related to the case. PROJECT INDUSTRY (REZ2025-00003, Brentsville District) — DEFERRED. From the May 20 2026 Planning Commission agenda: this is a request to rezone ±42.28 acres from M/T to M/T (re-rezone with proffer amendment of #PLN2003-00242) to allow data-center development with associated building-height increase up to 85 feet and an electrical substation up to 110 feet. The ±42.28-acre area is south of Wellington Road, addresses 8000-8041 Industrial Park Ct and 12901 Rollins Ford Rd (GPINs 7496-48-8861; 7496-58-0951; 7496-58-2739; 7496-58-4088; 7496-58-4226; 7496-58-4265; 7496-58-6207; 7496-58-6487; 7496-59-2613; 7496-68-0342). Designated I-4 Heavy Industrial with T-4 transect (0.57 to 1.38 FAR), partially within ERPO. Located within the Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District, E-Commerce Overlay District, and Airport Safety Overlay District. Case was deferred to date certain from 4/22/2026.

PRINCE WILLIAM COUNTY BOARD OF COUNTY SUPERVISORS — POLITICAL COMPOSITION (during the relevant 2023-2026 votes). Chair: Hon. Deshundra Jefferson (At-Large, Democratic majority chair through 2025-2026, voted AGAINST Hornbaker). Other supervisors active in the period: Vice Chair Andrea O. Bailey (Potomac District, Democratic); Victor S. Angry (Neabsco District, Democratic); Kenny A. Boddye (Occoquan District, Democratic, abstained on Digital Gateway); Yesli Vega (Coles District, Republican, voted AGAINST Hornbaker); George Stewart (Gainesville District, Republican, voted AGAINST Hornbaker); plus the Brentsville and Woodbridge representatives. PRINCE WILLIAM COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION — COMPOSITION (during 2025-2026 period). Chair Qwendolyn N. Brown; Vice-Chair Karla Justice (voted to DENY Hornbaker); Members: Christopher Carroll (Brentsville, voted to DENY Hornbaker), Brian Landrum, Blake Ross (voted to DENY Hornbaker), Mark Scheufler (voted to DENY Hornbaker), Raheel Sheikh (absent from Hornbaker), Michael Sherman. Earlier 2025 composition included Chair Juan McPhail (voted to APPROVE Hornbaker), Cynthia Moses-Nedd (voted to APPROVE Hornbaker). Across both bodies, Brentsville-area representation (Carroll on PC, traditionally rural-leaning) has been the most reliable NO vote on data-center actions in the Brentsville magisterial district. The Hornbaker decision split shows the PC opposing data centers outside DCOZ while a sufficient BOCS majority overrules and approves them anyway — relevant pattern for Vira's permitting model.

PERMITTING PATTERNS RELEVANT TO VIRA READINESS SCORING (synthesis from 2023-2026 PWC actions). 1) DCOZ overlay is the strongest single zoning signal. The 2019 administrative removal of the Hornbaker parcel from DCOZ was explicitly cited by Planning Commissioners as grounds for denial; that history is in the county record. Parcels outside DCOZ that pursue DC use face higher SUP burden and more PC opposition, even when BOCS ultimately approves. 2) Inside-DCOZ rezoning (Project Industry REZ2025-00003) goes through more smoothly when the parcel is already M/T zoned and the only requested change is a proffer amendment and height increase. The deferral history (4/22/2026 → 5/20/2026) does signal friction even within DCOZ. 3) Building height matters. Multiple recent cases requested 80-110 foot heights and 110-foot substations, which exceed by-right limits — each height modification adds a procedural hook for opposition. 4) Magisterial-district matters more than just population. Brentsville (rural, west) and Gainesville (Manassas Battlefield-adjacent) both show high political opposition to DC. Coles and Occoquan (mid-county) have approved DC at 5-3 / 4-3 margins. Woodbridge and Potomac (east) skew toward DC support as part of the Innovation District / Mid-County activity. 5) Generator + substation + transmission proffers are now standard. Hornbaker's last-minute Pegasus-substation proffer (no new transmission required) was decisive in pulling the 4th vote. 6) Litigation risk on procedural grounds is real. PW Digital Gateway was held void ab initio on a public-notice technicality before being stayed on appeal — a parcel sitting in a litigated rezoning area carries ongoing development uncertainty even after BOCS approval. 7) Opposition speaker count at PC hearings is the most directly-measurable political-risk signal. Hornbaker had 4 distinct topical concerns (electricity, health, noise, residential adjacency) raised by named speakers — these became the Vira opp_speakers / opp_topics_n fields. Other 2025 cases (Mid-County, GMU edge) likely had similar counts but transcripts are not publicly indexed. 8) BOCS appeal/litigation funding (e.g., $400K Apr 2026 vote for Digital Gateway defense) is a forward signal that the county will continue to defend prior approvals even as composition shifts.
